lesson.title: How the Web Works: HTTP, Browsers and the MEAN Architecture
objectives: Explain what happens between typing a URL and seeing a rendered page.
Describe the structure of an HTTP request and response, including methods, headers and status codes.
Map each MEAN layer (MongoDB, Express, Angular, Node.js) to its role in a request.
Distinguish client-side rendering, server-side rendering and APIs.
Parse a raw HTTP request and reason about its parts.
lesson.definition: The web is a client-server system in which a browser (the client) sends HTTP requests to a server and receives HTTP responses containing HTML, JSON, images or other resources. The MEAN stack is a JavaScript-everywhere architecture for such systems: Angular runs in the browser, Node.js with Express handles HTTP on the server, and MongoDB stores data as JSON-like documents.

theory.heading: From URL to rendered page
theory.body: When a user opens https://codinghub.in/courses, the browser first resolves the domain to an IP address with DNS, opens a TCP connection (or QUIC for HTTP/3), performs a TLS handshake for HTTPS, and then sends an HTTP request. The server replies with a response; the browser parses the HTML, builds the DOM, downloads CSS and JavaScript, builds the CSSOM, runs scripts and paints pixels. Interviewers ask this question to see whether you understand every layer rather than only the framework you use.
points: DNS lookup: domain name to IP address (with browser, OS and resolver caches).
Connection: TCP plus TLS handshake, or QUIC for HTTP/3.
HTTP request and response exchange.
Parsing and rendering: DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint.
JavaScript execution, which in a single-page app then fetches data from APIs.

theory.heading: Anatomy of HTTP
theory.body: HTTP is a stateless, text-oriented request-response protocol (HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 frame it in binary, but the semantics are the same). A request has a method, a target path with optional query string, a protocol version, headers and an optional body. A response has a status code, headers and an optional body. Statelessness is why sessions, cookies and tokens exist: each request must carry whatever the server needs to identify the user.
points: Methods: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove), OPTIONS (CORS preflight).
Status classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
Important headers: Host, Content-Type, Authorization, Cookie, Cache-Control, Accept.
Safe methods do not change state; idempotent methods give the same result when repeated (GET, PUT, DELETE).

theory.heading: The MEAN architecture
theory.body: In a MEAN application the Angular single-page app is downloaded once and then talks to a REST or GraphQL API over HTTP, usually exchanging JSON. Express is a minimal framework on top of Node.js's http module that maps routes to handler functions. Node.js runs JavaScript on the server with a non-blocking event loop, which suits I/O-heavy APIs. MongoDB stores documents in BSON, so data can flow from database to browser with little transformation.
points: Angular: UI, routing in the browser, forms, calling the API with HttpClient.
Express: routing, middleware (auth, validation, logging), error handling.
Node.js: the runtime, event loop, file and network I/O.
MongoDB: document storage, indexes, aggregation; accessed through Mongoose or the native driver.

theory.heading: Rendering strategies
theory.body: A classic Angular app uses client-side rendering (CSR): the server sends an almost empty index.html plus JavaScript bundles, and the browser builds the page. This gives app-like navigation but a slower first paint and weaker SEO. Angular SSR renders the first view on a Node.js server and then hydrates it in the browser, improving first contentful paint and crawlability. Static pre-rendering (SSG) generates HTML at build time for pages that rarely change.
points: CSR: fast navigation after load, heavier first load.
SSR with hydration: better first paint and SEO, needs a Node server.
SSG/prerendering: cheapest to serve, only for mostly static content.

theory.heading: Why full-stack JavaScript matters, and its limits
theory.body: Using one language across the stack lets teams share types (with TypeScript), validation logic and developers. JSON is native to every layer. The trade-offs are real: Node.js is not ideal for CPU-heavy work without worker threads, MongoDB's flexible schema needs discipline (Mongoose schemas, validation) and Angular has a steeper learning curve than lighter libraries. Good candidates mention these trade-offs instead of claiming MEAN is best for everything.
points: Advantages: one language, shared models, JSON end to end, large ecosystem.
Limitations: CPU-bound work, schema discipline, framework complexity.

example.title: A request travelling through the MEAN layers
example.body: An Angular component asks a service for courses. The service calls HttpClient, which sends GET /api/courses?page=2. Express matches the route, a handler queries MongoDB through Mongoose, and the JSON response flows back to the component, which renders it. Each layer has a single responsibility.

takeaways: A page load involves DNS, connection and TLS setup, HTTP exchange, then parsing and rendering.
HTTP is stateless; cookies or tokens carry identity between requests.
Know the main methods, status code classes and which methods are safe or idempotent.
MEAN = Angular in the browser, Express on Node.js for the API, MongoDB for documents.
CSR, SSR with hydration and prerendering trade first-load speed, SEO and server cost.
Mention the limits of MEAN (CPU-heavy work, schema discipline) to show balanced judgement.

interview.question: What happens when you type a URL into the browser and press Enter?
interview.answer: The browser checks caches and resolves the domain with DNS, opens a TCP (or QUIC) connection, completes a TLS handshake for HTTPS, sends an HTTP request, receives the response, parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, runs JavaScript, then performs layout and paint.
interview.explanation: A strong answer is ordered and mentions caching, TLS and the rendering pipeline. For a MEAN role, add that an Angular SPA then makes API calls for data.

interview.question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
interview.answer: PUT replaces the whole resource with the representation sent and is idempotent. PATCH applies a partial update; it is not guaranteed to be idempotent (for example an 'increment' patch).
interview.explanation: Interviewers look for the replace-versus-partial distinction and correct use of the word idempotent.

interview.question: Explain 401 versus 403.
interview.answer: 401 Unauthorized means the request lacks valid authentication (no token or an expired one). 403 Forbidden means the user is authenticated but not allowed to perform the action.
interview.explanation: Linking it to practice helps: an Angular interceptor redirects to login on 401 but shows an 'access denied' message on 403.

interview.question: Why is HTTP called stateless, and how do web apps keep users logged in?
interview.answer: Each request is independent; the server keeps no memory of earlier requests at the protocol level. Apps add state with session cookies (server-side session store) or tokens such as JWTs sent in a header or cookie on every request.
interview.explanation: Mentioning both server sessions and tokens, and that the choice affects scaling, sets up the authentication discussion later.

interview.question: When would you add server-side rendering to an Angular application?
interview.answer: When first-load performance or SEO matters, such as public marketing or catalogue pages. Angular SSR renders HTML on the server and hydrates it in the browser. For logged-in dashboards, CSR is often enough.
interview.explanation: Good answers weigh the cost (a Node server, browser-only APIs must be guarded) against the benefit, rather than recommending SSR everywhere.

practice.title: Parse a raw HTTP request
practice.objective: Understand the parts of an HTTP request (request line, query string, headers, body) by parsing one the way a server such as Node's http module does.
practice.statement: The global string stdin holds a raw HTTP request: a request line, header lines, an empty line, then an optional body. Print the method, the path without the query string, the query parameters, the Host header, the Content-Type header and the body length. Header names are case-insensitive. Query values must be URL-decoded ('+' means a space). If the request line does not have exactly three parts or the third part is not an HTTP version (HTTP/ followed by a digit), print only '400 Bad Request'.
practice.input_format: Request line, then 'Name: value' header lines, then an empty line, then optional body text. The empty line may be missing when there are no headers or body.
practice.output_format:
Six lines:
METHOD <method>
PATH <path>
QUERY <k=v pairs joined by '; '> or QUERY none
HOST <host> or HOST missing
CONTENT-TYPE <value> or CONTENT-TYPE none
BODY <number of characters in the body>

example.input:
GET /api/courses?page=2&sort=title HTTP/1.1
Host: codinghub.in
Accept: application/json
example.output:
METHOD GET
PATH /api/courses
QUERY page=2; sort=title
HOST codinghub.in
CONTENT-TYPE none
BODY 0

constraints: Treat CRLF and LF line endings the same.
Trailing newlines at the end of the body are not counted.
A query parameter without '=' has an empty value.
Do not use require or process; read the global stdin string.
explanation: Normalise line endings, then split the text at the first empty line: everything before is the head, everything after is the body.
Split the request line on whitespace; it must have three parts and the third must start with HTTP/ and a digit, otherwise answer 400.
Separate path and query at the first '?', and decode each value (turning '+' into a space first).
Store headers in an object keyed by the lower-cased name, because HTTP header names are case-insensitive.
Print the six labelled lines, using defaults when a header or the query is absent.

quiz.question: Which HTTP status code best fits a request with a valid token from a user who lacks permission for the resource?
quiz.explanation: 403 means the identity is known but not allowed. 401 is for missing or invalid authentication.

quiz.question: In the MEAN stack, which layer is responsible for matching URL paths to handler functions on the server?
quiz.explanation: Express provides server-side routing and middleware on top of Node.js. Angular's router works in the browser.

quiz.question: Which of these HTTP methods is idempotent?
quiz.explanation: Repeating the same PUT leaves the resource in the same state. POST creates a new resource each time, and an increment PATCH changes the result on repeat.

quiz.question: A public Angular product catalogue ranks poorly in search engines and shows a blank page for a second on slow phones. What change helps most?
options: Switch MongoDB to a relational database
Increase the HTTP cache time of the API
Enable Angular SSR with hydration for those pages
quiz.explanation: SSR sends rendered HTML, improving first paint and crawlability; hydration then makes it interactive.

quiz.question: Given the request line 'GET /api/users?role=admin HTTP/1.1', what does Express put in req.path and req.query.role?
quiz.explanation: req.path excludes the query string, and Express's query parser maps role=admin to the string 'admin'.

lesson.title: JavaScript Core: Types, Scope, Hoisting and Closures
objectives: Distinguish primitive and reference types and predict copying and comparison behaviour.
Explain var, let and const in terms of scope, hoisting and the temporal dead zone.
Describe how closures capture variables and use them for private state.
Explain how the value of 'this' is decided and how arrow functions differ.
Answer classic output-prediction questions on coercion and equality.
lesson.definition: JavaScript is a dynamically typed language with seven primitive types (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol) and objects, which are passed around by reference. Scope decides where a variable is visible; a closure is a function together with the variables from its surrounding scope that it keeps alive after that scope has finished executing.

theory.heading: Primitive versus reference values
theory.body: Primitives are immutable and compared by value: copying a number copies the value. Objects, arrays and functions are reference values: a variable holds a reference, so assigning it to another variable makes both point to the same object. This explains why mutating an array inside a function is visible to the caller, and why Angular's OnPush change detection (Day 20) relies on replacing objects rather than mutating them.
points: typeof null is 'object' (a historical bug); use value === null to test for null.
=== compares without type coercion; == coerces (for example '5' == 5 is true).
Two different objects are never ===, even with identical contents.
const prevents reassignment of the variable, not mutation of the object it points to.

theory.heading: Scope, hoisting and the temporal dead zone
theory.body: JavaScript has global, function and block scope. During the creation phase of an execution context, declarations are registered before code runs (hoisting). var declarations are hoisted and initialised to undefined, and are function-scoped. let and const are block-scoped and hoisted but not initialised, so accessing them before the declaration line throws a ReferenceError: that window is the temporal dead zone. Function declarations are hoisted with their body; function expressions follow the rules of the variable they are assigned to.
points: Prefer const by default, let when reassignment is needed, avoid var.
Block scope makes let safe in loops: each iteration gets a fresh binding.
Lexical scope: a function sees variables where it is defined, not where it is called.

theory.heading: Closures
theory.body: When a function is created, it keeps a reference to its lexical environment. If an inner function outlives its outer function (it is returned, stored or used as a callback), the variables it uses stay alive. Closures give private state without classes, power factories, memoisation, debouncing and partial application, and are everywhere in callback-based Node.js code and RxJS operators.
points: Data privacy: variables in the outer function cannot be reached from outside.
Function factories: makeMultiplier(3) returns a function that remembers 3.
Common bug: var in a loop with setTimeout prints the final value for every callback.
Memory: closures keep captured variables alive, so avoid capturing large objects unnecessarily.

theory.heading: How 'this' is determined
theory.body: For normal functions, 'this' is decided by how the function is called, not where it is written. A method call obj.fn() sets this to obj; a plain call fn() gives undefined in strict mode (modules and classes are strict); new sets this to the new object; call, apply and bind set it explicitly. Arrow functions do not have their own 'this' and use the one from the enclosing scope, which is why they are used for callbacks inside class methods in Angular components.
points: Losing 'this': passing obj.method as a callback detaches it from obj.
Fix with an arrow function, bind, or a class field arrow function.
Arrow functions cannot be used as constructors and have no arguments object.

theory.heading: Type coercion pitfalls
theory.body: Operators coerce operands: + concatenates if either side is a string, while -, * and / convert to numbers. Falsy values are false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined and NaN; everything else, including '0', [] and {}, is truthy. NaN is the only value not equal to itself, so use Number.isNaN. The nullish coalescing operator ?? only falls back on null or undefined, unlike || which also replaces 0 and ''.
points: Optional chaining user?.address?.city avoids errors on missing objects.

example.title: A closure that keeps state private
example.body: createCounter returns two functions that share the same count variable. Nothing outside can modify count directly, and each call to createCounter creates a separate, independent count. This is the module pattern that predates classes and ES modules.

use_cases.title: Encapsulated modules
use_cases.description: Factories and module patterns expose a small API while keeping helper state private.

use_cases.title: Event handlers and callbacks
use_cases.description: Handlers remember the item or ID they were created for, for example a click handler per list row.

use_cases.title: Memoisation and caching
use_cases.description: A wrapper function keeps a private cache Map so repeated calls with the same input are fast.

use_cases.title: Middleware configuration
use_cases.description: Express middleware factories such as rateLimit({ max: 100 }) return a function that closes over the options.

demonstration.description: Predict the output of the classic loop question. With var there is one shared i, and the callbacks run after the loop finishes. With let each iteration has its own binding, so each closure captures a different value.
demonstration.output:
var 3
var 3
var 3
let 0
let 1
let 2

takeaways: Primitives are copied by value; objects are shared by reference and compared by identity.
var is function-scoped and initialised to undefined; let and const are block-scoped with a temporal dead zone.
A closure keeps its outer variables alive and is the basis of private state and factories.
'this' depends on the call site, except in arrow functions, which inherit it lexically.
Use === and ?? to avoid surprising coercion.

interview.question: What is the difference between var, let and const?
interview.answer: var is function-scoped, can be redeclared and is hoisted as undefined. let and const are block-scoped, cannot be redeclared in the same scope and are in the temporal dead zone until declared. const cannot be reassigned, though an object it refers to can still be mutated.
interview.explanation: Mention scope, hoisting, the TDZ and the const-mutation nuance; those four points separate a complete answer from a partial one.

interview.question: What is a closure? Give a practical use.
interview.answer: A closure is a function bundled with references to the variables in the scope where it was created, which it can still use after that scope has returned. Uses include private state (a counter or bank account), function factories, memoisation and configured middleware.
interview.explanation: Interviewers want a definition plus a real use. Writing a small factory on the whiteboard is the strongest proof.

interview.question: What does this code print: console.log(typeof null, typeof [], typeof NaN)?
interview.answer: 'object object number'. typeof null is a long-standing quirk, arrays are objects (use Array.isArray), and NaN is of type number.
interview.explanation: These quirks are favourite screening questions; follow up by naming the correct checks (=== null, Array.isArray, Number.isNaN).

interview.question: Why might 'this' be undefined inside a method used as a callback, and how do you fix it?
interview.answer: Passing obj.method as a callback calls it as a plain function, so 'this' is undefined in strict mode. Fix it by wrapping in an arrow function (() => obj.method()), using obj.method.bind(obj), or defining the method as an arrow-function class field.
interview.explanation: This shows you understand that 'this' is set at call time; in Angular it appears with setTimeout or third-party callbacks inside components.

interview.question: Can closures cause memory leaks? How?
interview.answer: Yes. A long-lived closure, such as an event listener or an interval callback that is never removed, keeps every captured variable reachable, including large objects or DOM nodes, so they cannot be garbage-collected. Remove listeners, clear intervals and unsubscribe when the owner is destroyed.
interview.explanation: Linking this to Angular (unsubscribing in ngOnDestroy or using takeUntilDestroyed) shows senior-level awareness.

practice.title: Private bank accounts with closures
practice.objective: Use closures to hold private state that can only be changed through a controlled API.
practice.statement: Implement createAccount(initial) that returns an object with deposit, withdraw, getBalance and getHistory functions. The balance and history must live in closure variables, not object properties. Then process commands, one per line: 'open <name> <amount>', 'deposit <name> <amount>', 'withdraw <name> <amount>', 'balance <name>' and 'history <name>'. Print output only for balance, history and errors.
practice.input_format: One command per line. Names are single words; amounts are numbers. Blank lines are ignored.
practice.output_format: balance prints '<name>: <balance>'. history prints '<name>: ' followed by entries such as +50 and -30 separated by spaces, or '<name>: no transactions'. Errors print '<name>: unknown account', '<name>: already exists', '<name>: invalid amount' (amount not greater than 0) or '<name>: insufficient funds'.

deposit alice 50
withdraw alice 500
withdraw alice 30
balance alice
history alice

constraints: Opening balance is a number of at least 0 and is not recorded in history.
A failed deposit or withdrawal does not change the balance or history.
Accounts are independent: each open creates a new closure.
explanation: createAccount declares balance and history inside the function; the returned methods close over them, so no outside code can touch them directly.
deposit and withdraw validate the amount first (!(amount > 0) also rejects NaN) and return an error string instead of changing state.
getHistory returns a copy so callers cannot mutate the private array.
A Map stores one account object per name; each open call creates a fresh closure with its own state.
The command loop prints balances, history and any error string returned by the account.

quiz.explanation: var a is hoisted and initialised to undefined. let b is in the temporal dead zone until its declaration, so reading it throws a ReferenceError.

quiz.question: Which statement about closures is correct?
options: Closures are created only by calling bind()
An inner function keeps access to variables of its outer scope even after the outer function returns
A closure copies the outer variables' values at creation time and never sees later changes
Closures only exist when a function is declared with the 'function' keyword
quiz.explanation: Closures keep a live reference to the outer environment, so they see the current value of captured variables, and arrow functions form closures too.

quiz.question: What do these || and ?? expressions print?
quiz.explanation: || falls back on any falsy value, including 0. ?? only falls back on null or undefined, so it keeps 0.

quiz.question: Inside a class method you call setTimeout(this.save, 1000), and save() throws 'Cannot read properties of undefined'. What is the best fix?
options: Pass an arrow function: setTimeout(() => this.save(), 1000)
Change const to let in the class
quiz.explanation: Passing this.save detaches the method from the instance. An arrow function keeps the lexical 'this' and calls save as a method.

quiz.explanation: Arrays are reference values: copy points to the same array, so the push is visible through list and both variables are identical.

lesson.title: Modern JavaScript (ES6+): Destructuring, Spread, Modules and Array Methods
objectives: Use destructuring with defaults and renaming for objects, arrays and function parameters.
Apply spread and rest syntax to copy, merge and collect values immutably.
Choose between map, filter, reduce, find, some and every for data transformations.
Explain ES modules (import/export) and how they differ from CommonJS.
Use classes, template literals, optional chaining and Map/Set where they fit.
lesson.definition: ES6 (ECMAScript 2015) and the yearly releases after it added the syntax modern JavaScript and TypeScript code relies on: let/const, arrow functions, classes, template literals, destructuring, spread/rest, modules, Map/Set, promises and later async/await, optional chaining and nullish coalescing. Angular, Express and Mongoose code is written almost entirely in this style.

theory.heading: Destructuring and default values
theory.body: Destructuring unpacks values from objects or arrays into variables in one statement. It can rename (const { id: courseId } = course), provide defaults used when a value is undefined (const { page = 1 } = query), and work in function parameters, which makes an options object self-documenting. Array destructuring is positional and is used for swaps and for tuple-like returns.
points: Object: const { title, price = 0 } = course;
Array: const [first, , third] = list;
Parameters: function list({ page = 1, limit = 10 } = {}) { ... }
Defaults apply only for undefined, not for null.

theory.heading: Spread and rest
theory.body: The same three dots mean two different things. Spread expands an iterable or object into individual elements or properties; rest collects the remaining ones into an array or object. Spread creates a shallow copy, which is the basis of immutable updates in Angular state management: { ...state, loading: true } produces a new object, so reference checks notice the change. Nested objects are still shared, so deep changes need nested spreads or structuredClone.
points: Merge: const config = { ...defaults, ...overrides }; later keys win.
Copy and append: const next = [...items, newItem];
Rest parameters: function sum(...nums) { ... }
Omit a key: const { password, ...safeUser } = user;

theory.heading: Array methods for data transformation
theory.body: Declarative array methods replace most for loops in application code. map transforms each element, filter keeps elements matching a condition, reduce folds the array into a single value (sum, grouping, lookup table), find returns the first match, and some/every answer yes-or-no questions. They do not mutate the source array (sort, reverse and splice do, which is why toSorted and toReversed were added in ES2023). Chaining them keeps code readable, but each step allocates a new array, so for very large datasets a single reduce or a loop can be faster.
points: map: same length, transformed values.
filter: subset; find: first match or undefined.
reduce: accumulate anything; always pass an initial value.
Object.entries, Object.fromEntries and Object.groupBy help with keyed data.

theory.heading: ES modules versus CommonJS
theory.body: ES modules use import and export, are statically analysable (enabling tree shaking in Angular builds), are always in strict mode and load asynchronously. CommonJS uses require and module.exports, loads synchronously and was Node.js's original system. Modern Node.js supports both: files ending in .mjs, or a package.json with "type": "module", are treated as ES modules. Angular and TypeScript code always uses ES module syntax.
points: Named exports: export function x() {}, imported with { x }.
Default export: one per module; import any name.
Dynamic import(): loads a module on demand, used for lazy-loaded Angular routes.

theory.heading: Other everyday features
theory.body: Classes provide constructor, methods, getters, static members and true private fields (#secret). Template literals interpolate expressions and span lines. Map keeps insertion order and allows any key type; Set stores unique values, making de-duplication a one-liner. Optional chaining (a?.b?.c) and nullish coalescing (x ?? fallback) make safe access to API responses concise.
points: Unique values: [...new Set(tags)].
Map vs object: any key type, size property, predictable iteration order.

lesson.title: Asynchronous JavaScript and the Event Loop
objectives: Explain why JavaScript needs an event loop despite running on a single thread.
Describe the call stack, the task (macrotask) queue and the microtask queue.
Predict the output order of code mixing synchronous logs, timers and promises.
Identify callback hell and the inversion-of-control problem of callbacks.
Explain how a long synchronous task blocks rendering in the browser and requests in Node.js.
lesson.definition: The event loop is the mechanism that lets single-threaded JavaScript perform non-blocking work. Synchronous code runs on the call stack; slow operations (timers, network, file I/O) are handed to the host environment, and their callbacks are queued. Whenever the stack is empty, the loop first drains the microtask queue (promise reactions, queueMicrotask) and then takes the next task (macrotask) such as a timer callback or an I/O event.

theory.heading: Single thread, non-blocking I/O
theory.body: A JavaScript engine executes one piece of code at a time on one call stack. If a network request blocked that thread, a browser tab would freeze and a Node.js server could serve only one client at a time. Instead, the host (the browser's Web APIs or Node's libuv) performs the waiting outside the JavaScript thread and later queues a callback. This model is why Node.js can handle thousands of concurrent connections with little memory, and also why one CPU-heavy loop stalls everything.
points: Call stack: frames of currently executing functions.
Host APIs: timers, fetch/XHR, DOM events, file system, sockets.
Queues: callbacks wait until the stack is empty.
Run-to-completion: a function is never interrupted by another callback.

theory.heading: Tasks versus microtasks
theory.body: There are two kinds of queues. Tasks (often called macrotasks) include setTimeout, setInterval, I/O callbacks and UI events; the loop takes one task per iteration. Microtasks include promise .then/.catch/.finally reactions, await continuations, queueMicrotask and MutationObserver. After every task, and after the initial script, the microtask queue is drained completely, including microtasks added while draining, before the next task or a render happens.
points: Order: synchronous code, then all microtasks, then one task, then all microtasks again.
setTimeout(fn, 0) means 'run as a task after at least 0 ms', never immediately.
An endless chain of microtasks starves timers and rendering.

theory.heading: Node.js event-loop phases
theory.body: Node.js's loop (libuv) cycles through phases: timers (expired setTimeout/setInterval), pending callbacks, poll (waiting for and running I/O callbacks), check (setImmediate) and close callbacks. Between callbacks Node drains process.nextTick callbacks first and then promise microtasks. Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always runs before a setTimeout(fn, 0); from the main module their order is not guaranteed.
points: process.nextTick runs before promise microtasks; overusing it can starve I/O.
setImmediate is for 'run after the current poll phase'.
CPU-heavy work belongs in worker_threads or a separate service.

theory.heading: Callbacks and their problems
theory.body: The original asynchronous pattern was passing a callback, and Node.js standardised error-first callbacks: callback(err, result). Nested sequential operations produce deeply indented 'callback hell', error handling must be repeated at every level, and you hand control to the called code, which might call your callback twice or never (inversion of control). Promises (Day 5) fix these by representing a future value as an object that settles exactly once.
points: Error-first convention: if (err) return handle(err);
Callback hell hurts readability and error propagation.
Promises and async/await flatten the code and centralise errors.

theory.heading: Why this matters in Angular
theory.body: Angular has traditionally used Zone.js to patch asynchronous APIs (timers, events, XHR) so it knows when a task finishes and can run change detection. Understanding tasks and microtasks explains why a value set in a setTimeout appears after the next check, why ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked errors happen, and why newer zoneless Angular relies on signals and explicit notifications instead of patching every async API.
points: Zone.js tracks async tasks and triggers change detection when they complete.
Zoneless apps schedule change detection from signal updates, events and markForCheck.

interview.question: What is the event loop?
interview.answer: It is the loop that coordinates the call stack and the callback queues. When the stack is empty it drains all microtasks, then takes the next task (timer, I/O, UI event) and runs it, repeating forever. This lets single-threaded JavaScript perform non-blocking I/O.
interview.explanation: Name the call stack, host APIs and both queues; a diagram on the whiteboard helps.

interview.question: What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks?
interview.answer: Macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, events) are taken one per loop iteration. Microtasks (promise reactions, queueMicrotask, await continuations) run in full after the current script or task, before the next macrotask and before rendering.
interview.explanation: Strong candidates add the starvation risk: recursively queued microtasks can block timers and painting.

interview.question: Does setTimeout(fn, 0) run immediately?
interview.answer: No. It queues fn as a task to run after at least 0 ms, once the current script and all pending microtasks have finished, and browsers may clamp nested timers to 4 ms.
interview.explanation: This is the standard trick question; explaining queue position, not delay, is the key.

interview.explanation: Mentioning the non-determinism from the main module shows real Node.js knowledge rather than a memorised list.

interview.explanation: This scenario checks that you understand non-blocking applies to I/O, not to CPU work.

days.title: Asynchronous JavaScript and the Event Loop
days.focus: The event loop is the mechanism that lets single-threaded JavaScript perform non-blocking work. Synchronous code runs on the call stack; slow operations (timers, network, file I/O) are handed to the host environment, and their callbacks are queued.
